name: Wendy Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, unions, AI firms or government. Your answers stay confidential. What is a normal workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy Usman, 58, and I've built and repaired power lines for years since my certificate and apprenticeship. I know the ordinary faults around East Quarry, but my pay is low for the job; I like handing power back to homes, and I keep the signed circuit sheet in reach on every call.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: A dentist bill took what little we had saved, and rent follows every month. My partner Dev works in a school kitchen with breaks between terms; our children are grown and paying their own way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the depot a quicker form might spare us a few minutes, but the cable still needs testing and repair. I know that part of the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't expect the small AI change to cost my job, but our money is tight already. My pay is low for line work, the dentist bill cleared our savings, and Dev's kitchen shifts change with the school term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep taking the normal repair rota and ask the supervisor about any safe extra shifts next month. In the first year Dev and I would stop buying lunch at the depot until we have one full month of bills saved again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel confident with a tester and worried when the rent date comes near. A quiet technology story doesn't pay the dentist bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What was the dentist bill for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A broken tooth turned into two visits, and the second payment used the last of our reserve. Our grown children brought soup round, but they have their own households to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use a note tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I haven't used AI tools and don't see a reason to start for a few minutes saved. I can read the signed circuit sheet and write the repair plainly.

say: I'd say **cable testing** and repair still need field workers.
I'd accept **quicker forms** if the signed record stays clear.
think: The **dentist bill** emptied our savings while my line pay stays low.
Dev's **term-time kitchen shifts** leave rent feeling uncertain even without major AI change.
do: Take the **normal repair rota** and ask about safe extra shifts next month.
Stop buying **depot lunches** until one month of bills is saved again.
feel: **Confident** at work, worried near the rent date.
S0.quote: A quiet technology story doesn't pay the dentist bill.
fieldNote: Wendy's **baseline money worry** comes from a dental cost, lower pay and Dev's variable school kitchen shifts.
She **never uses AI tools** and relies on the signed circuit sheet; field skill makes the job familiar, not the finances secure.

steps.text: Take normal repair shifts and ask the supervisor about safe extras
Stop buying depot lunches until one month of bills is saved

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell management to prove the new dispatch system on the worst local roads before changing staff hours. A route that looks short on a map can take us through a locked quarry gate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Field repairs should still need us for a while, but less dispatch time could mean fewer callouts. Those extra shifts often cover the weeks when Dev's school kitchen closes, and we have almost no reserve now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask our dispatcher to check any new route against the gate list before I drive it. In the first year I'd keep paid line shifts and delay replacing the still-working washing machine if callout pay falls twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy with the software and anxious about the extra pay. I'm not against a tool that works, but I'd need the dispatcher to show me the evidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where is the quarry gate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The East Quarry road bends behind a locked fence after dusk, and the truck cannot turn there. Our dispatcher knows the upper road has the key box.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train on the system yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch the dispatcher compare routes, but I won't pretend to use AI when I don't. If it passes the local checks, I can follow the printed direction.

say: I'd demand **local-road proof** on night calls before dispatch staffing changes at our depot.
I'd keep **dispatcher checks** on locked access gates.
think: Fewer **callout shifts** could cut the money covering Dev's school breaks.
Our **near-empty reserve** gives us little time to absorb that loss.
do: Ask dispatch to check **new routes** against the gate list before driving.
Keep **paid line shifts** and delay the washing machine after two lower callout payments.
feel: **Uneasy** about software and anxious about lost extra pay.
S1.quote: A route that looks short on a map can take us through a locked quarry gate.
fieldNote: Wendy links **callout pay** to school breaks in Dev's kitchen work, making dispatch changes a household income issue.
She requests **human route checking** and printed directions without claiming to use AI herself.

steps.text: Continue paid line shifts and ask dispatch to check gate access
Delay replacing the washing machine after two lower callout payments

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 can write a plan, but a crew still repairs lines until the robots arrive around 2031. By then I want the company to say exactly which repair shifts it plans to keep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 63 when robots can do my work, and I expect a serious cut in our line hours. Dev's kitchen work might face machines too, while we have less than a month's bills saved and only one other utility within commuting distance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the company for a written staffing timetable and the employment office for its list of paid electrical inspection courses. In 2029 I'd enroll if wages continue during training; during the first robot year I'd apply to the other utility and for posted inspection shifts here, and ask our grown son for a lift to interviews if needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lie awake thinking of two payslips shrinking together. I can make applications, but I cannot make a nearby employer create a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Dev we need to keep the rent money clear of any course fee. Our grown son can give a lift, not a second wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave line work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I need the paid shifts while they are here. I wouldn't resign on the hope that inspection jobs will exist in 2031.

say: I'd separate **2028 planning AI** from 2031 repair robots.
I'd demand a **written shift plan** before the robot rollout.
think: At **63**, I expect serious loss of line hours.
Dev's **kitchen wages** may also shrink while our savings cover less than a month.
do: Request **staffing dates** and paid-course information now.
Enroll if **training pays wages** in 2029, then apply for real utility and inspection jobs in 2031.
feel: **Sleepless** over two likely smaller payslips and few nearby jobs.
S2.quote: Our grown son can give a lift, not a second wage.
fieldNote: Wendy expects **large hour cuts** at the 2031 robot date and reports sleeplessness about both household wages.
Her **family support** is limited to interview transport; she will keep paid shifts and train only while wages continue.

steps.text: Request a written company staffing timetable for robot rollout
Enroll in inspection training in 2029 if wages continue
Apply to the other nearby utility and posted inspection shifts
Ask her grown son for transport to job interviews if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company five years gives it time to test robots and tell crews what jobs remain. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, then field robots around 2034, when I'll be 66.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 I might be able to retire, but I can't know without a real pension figure. We have less than a month saved now, and Dev's kitchen job may also change when physical machines improve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd request a written pension estimate and ask the supervisor to show the company's field robot test results. In 2032 I'd take a paid inspection placement if one opens; when robots arrive in 2034 I'd keep any safe paid line shifts and apply for inspection work if the pension won't cover rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less rushed and still worried. A longer warning helps me ask questions, but it doesn't create savings while the dentist bill is still being paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which figure would decide retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estimate after rent and medicines, with a low number for Dev's school breaks. I don't want the best working month used as our retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you test in a robot trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The East Quarry gate and the narrow space before the transformer. A machine that cannot turn its equipment safely there should stop and call a crew.

say: I'd ask for **field trial results** and a clear staffing plan before 2034.
I'd distinguish **2031 thinking AI** from later hands-on robots.
think: Retirement at **66** needs a verified pension after rent and medicines.
Dev's **kitchen work** and our thin savings leave little margin.
do: Get a **written pension estimate** and review company robot trials this year.
Take a **paid placement** if offered in 2032; keep line shifts and seek inspection work in 2034.
feel: **Less rushed**, still worried about bills and uncertain income.
S3.quote: A longer warning helps me ask questions, but it doesn't create savings while the dentist bill is still being paid.
fieldNote: Wendy's **2034 retirement question** depends on an actual pension estimate and low household income in school breaks.
Her **East Quarry test** concerns physical access, while paid placements and continued line shifts are conditional on openings.

steps.text: Request written pension figures and company robot trial results
Take a paid inspection placement in 2032 if one opens
Keep safe paid line shifts in 2034 if available
Apply for posted inspection work if pension income falls short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now let's talk about AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the younger crew ten years is enough to keep proper circuit records and make companies state the rules for robot repairs. Thinking AI arrives in 2036, and robots reach the pole around 2039, when I'll be 71.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope to retire before 71, but the pension number is missing and our savings are almost gone. The dentist payment and school-break income are problems now, even if the machine arrives much later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep paid field shifts and get the pension statement, then clear the dentist balance. In 2037 Dev and I would choose a retirement date only if a low-income budget covers rent; in 2039 I'd seek a posted inspection shift if the figures still don't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calmer about the robot timetable and anxious about this year's money. Ten years gives us a chance, provided the wages keep coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you build any reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: After the dentist balance is gone, I'd set aside twelve from any real weekend callout. I won't count on a callout that hasn't been assigned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children help you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They could help pack, but moving would need a paid job at the other end. I wouldn't put rent on their shoulders.

say: I'd ask for **clear repair rules** and circuit records over the decade.
I'd note **2039 robots** reach field work when I'll be 71.
think: Retirement before **71** depends on an unknown pension figure.
Our **dentist balance** and school-break income remain urgent now.
do: Keep **paid field shifts**, obtain a pension statement and clear dental debt.
Save **twelve from real callouts** after the debt clears, then review retirement in 2037.
feel: **Calmer** about robots, anxious about current money.
S4.quote: I won't count on a callout that hasn't been assigned.
fieldNote: Wendy's **long robot runway** does not resolve current dental debt or variable school-break household income.
Her **conditional savings** begin after debt clearance and depend on real, assigned weekend callouts.

steps.text: Keep paid field shifts and clear the dentist balance
Save twelve from each assigned weekend callout after debt clears
Set a 2037 retirement date only if low-income figures cover rent
Apply for posted inspection work if retirement income falls short

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots could cut my repair shifts in 2031 while Dev's kitchen work is also exposed. I need a written staffing plan, paid training, real nearby vacancies and help getting to interviews.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether the company's new job exists on a rota with a wage. A course title won't cover our rent.

headlineQuote: A course title won't cover our rent.
portrait: Wendy is a **58-year-old experienced lineworker** with a certificate and apprenticeship, lower pay and less than one month saved.
Her **dentist debt** and Dev's term-time kitchen work make even small changes feel costly at home.
She **never uses AI tools** and checks routes through dispatch, signed circuit sheets and observed field access.
The **2031 robot date** alarms her because she expects a serious hour cut with few nearby alternatives.
More warning allows **pension checks** from real callouts, while paid repairs remain essential.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries Wendy most because 2031 robots could cut her shifts while Dev's kitchen job also faces machines.
whatWouldHelp: She needs a **written staffing plan**, paid training, real nearby vacancies and interview transport.
